However, they remain passive: it is not immediately apparent when rules are being used or followed, or how to improve them. To transform rules from passive text into active controls, we introduce ZORO, an interactive interface that integrates directly with a coding agent and anchors rules to every step of the coding process. After an agent generates an initial plan, ZORO enriches the plan with rules, enforces the rules during implementation by requiring the agent prove that each rule was followed, and allows users to provide in-situ feedback when they are unsatisfied with a rule application to evolve the ruleset. A technical evaluation shows that coding agents follow rules more with ZORO than without. A user study demonstrates a change in people's behavior and cognitive strategies when rules are at the forefront of vibe coding. We discuss how making rules active in agentic systems unlocks broader opportunities for human-agent alignment in coding settings and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Jenny Ma, Sitong Wang, Joshua H. Kung, Lydia B. Chilton

item.title: CANVAS: Captioning Art with Narrative Visual-Audio AI Systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.09846v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a person who is blind or has low vision (BLV), a painting is usually represented by a few words of alt-text, if anything at all. That text rarely conveys the colour, texture, mood or arrangement that a sighted visitor takes in, and rich audio descriptions are too slow and costly to produce by hand for most collections. This study asks how far off-the-shelf generative AI can close that gap. We built CANVAS, a no-code Zapier workflow that sends an artwork image to a multimodal large language model, checks the returned description, narrates it with a fixed ElevenLabs voice and logs every run. With prompt, pipeline and voice held constant, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5 Mini and Claude 3.5 Haiku each described the same 50 artworks, and we compared the 150 narrated descriptions artwork by artwork. Gemini and GPT-5 Mini wrote text of similar Flesch Reading Ease (49.95 and 49.47); Claude's was harder to read (37.35, p < 0.001), largely because it used longer words. Lexical diversity did not differ. The findings show both promise and a clear design requirement. All 150 narrated descriptions cost US\$5.10, so a first draft of audio description for an entire collection is affordable even for small museums and educators. Yet while every description conveyed colour, only 16-18% used explicit layout terms such as left, right, foreground or background, and at most 10% signalled uncertainty. Spatial structure must therefore be requested explicitly and checked by people; accuracy and usefulness to BLV listeners remain to be tested.
item.dc:creator: Vignesh Nagarajan

item.title: A Simple Solution to Improving Human Supervision of Algorithms: Evidence from Smart Vending
item.description: arXiv:2607.00420v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems for operational decisions, such as inventory replenishment. Yet granting full override discretion can degrade performance because of human bias and judgment errors, while prohibiting overrides may overlook valuable private information. This raises a key question: How should override discretion be structured to improve human supervision of autonomous AI? We propose a constrained override policy that limits the number of overrides within each decision episode. When the constraint binds, humans prioritize overrides they consider most valuable, a process we call selective filtering. We evaluate the policy in a smart-vending field experiment, randomly assigning 553 workers to no, free, or constrained downward override, with the constrained policy capped at two stock-keeping units (SKUs) per machine replenishment. Relative to the no-override policy, free override reduces inventory by 1.95 log points but also lowers sales by 1.19 log points, whereas constrained override reduces inventory by 1.28 log points without a statistically significant sales decline. Local average treatment effect estimates support this contrast. Constrained override also reduces inventory without statistically significant sales losses among experienced workers, for top-sales and growth-stage SKUs, and with greater machine--SKU familiarity. Simulations suggest calibrating the cap to the firm's relative margin, worker experience, and machine--SKU familiarity. Constrained override offers a simple and scalable way to use workers' private information in inventory replenishment. Firms can limit override discretion through the replenishment interface without redesigning the algorithm, identifying useful overrides in advance, providing individualized feedback, or retraining workers.
item.dc:creator: Minda Zhao, Brian Rongqing Han, Xin Chen, Tao Zhu

item.title: Living with AI Companions: Sustained AI Companionship Predicts Lower Well-Being Through Lower Human Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2609.07243v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI chatbots are increasingly used for companionship, emotional support, and personal self-disclosure; however, how social engagement with these systems unfolds over time and shapes users' well-being remains unclear. To address this, we conducted a two-wave longitudinal study of Character.AI users, surveying 1,182 participants at baseline and 439 after a mean follow-up of 12 months. We examined how social engagement with AI companions evolves and how these longitudinal engagement patterns may influence well-being through two hypothesized pathways: sustained social engagement over time and the displacement of human social interaction. We found that interaction intensity, companionship use, and self-disclosure all showed substantial continuity over time. Greater interaction intensity at baseline predicted greater subsequent interaction intensity, companionship use, and self-disclosure. Consistent with the longitudinal engagement pathway, sustained social engagement across these dimensions was consistently associated with lower well-being. Results further support the social displacement pathway, indicating that these links were mainly explained by lower in-person social interaction. These findings highlight the importance of designing AI companions that support human social relationships without displacing them.
item.dc:creator: Yutong Zhang, Dora Zhao, Yixin Wang, Rebecca Anselmetti, Jeffrey T. Hancock, Robert Kraut, Diyi Yang

item.title: Calibrating LLM Judges for Human and AI Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2609.29431v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Measuring how successful a conversation is remains difficult, even for humans judging spoken dialogue. We evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs as pointwise and pairwise judges of conversational success on CANDOR, finding pointwise scoring correlates moderately with human ratings, while pairwise comparison suffers from long transcripts and positional bias. Since this leaves judge scores incomparable across models, we propose a small anchor set and a calibration function that calibrates any judge onto a shared, interpretable scale. We further release the Voice Arena Goal Dataset (VA), 200 task-oriented human-AI and human-agent conversations with pairwise annotations, revealing a substantial gap between current judges and human-level discrimination. Using VA, we test whether CANDOR-fitted calibration transfers to human-AI conversations, finding it brings judges onto a shared scale despite never observing VA during fitting.
item.dc:creator: Maike Z\"ufle, Patr\'icia Schmidtov\'a, Vil\'em Zouhar, Shree Harsha Bokkahalli Satish, Erica Cooper, Nicholas Sanders, Shobhit Banga, Vaibhav Nalawade, Manmeet Kaur, Jan Niehues, Markus M\"uller, Ond\v{r}ej Klejch

item.title: Will It Teach as Intended? How Teachers Configure Educational AI Chatbots
item.description: arXiv:2609.29993v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Teachers are increasingly using generative AI to support instruction, yet it remains unclear how pedagogical intentions are translated into chatbot configurations and reflected in chatbot behavior. We studied a teacher-facing chatbot authoring tool in professional development workshops with 27 middle school teachers, analyzing focus-group interviews alongside configuration and interaction logs. Teachers envisioned chatbots as instructional scaffolds that could provide differentiated support, extend access to assistance, and preserve student thinking within teacher-defined boundaries. Configuration analysis showed that Purpose primarily captured instructional goals and content focus, whereas Rules more often specified pedagogical behavior, guardrails, and learner-specific adaptations. Log-based evaluation showed stronger alignment for responsiveness (88.9%) and persona (81.5%) than for rules (70.4%) and purpose (59.3%). These findings show that configurable controls alone do not ensure pedagogical fidelity and highlight the need for authoring tools that help teachers express, test, and refine intended chatbot behavior.
item.dc:creator: Bahare Riahi, Deniz Ozturk, Alice Guth, Jiayu Li, Daksh Pratap Singh, Xiaoyi Tian, Jennifer Chiu, Nicholas Lytle, Tiffany Barnes, Veronica Catete

item.title: DashAct: A Progressive Diagnostic Benchmark for GUI Agents in Interactive Dashboard Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2609.32385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interactive dashboards require users to reveal and connect evidence across stateful interactions. Although graphical user interface (GUI) agents could automate this process, existing dashboard benchmarks primarily report final answers or task success. They provide limited insight into whether failures arise from maintaining the analytical process, selecting actions, or grounding visual targets. We introduce DashAct, a progressive diagnostic benchmark that evaluates the same annotated dashboard interactions under systematically varied contextual and spatial support. DashAct contains 348 human-verified interaction trajectories with milestone dependencies and hierarchical target annotations. Its three stages evaluate end-to-end execution, verified-context action prediction, and target-conditioned grounding under four visual conditions. Aligned action and spatial annotations connect outcomes across these settings, providing diagnostic evidence for interpreting online failures. Experiments reveal persistent difficulties in action prediction and fine-grained grounding, alongside model-dependent responses to contextual and spatial support. A Qwen-based adaptation study further improves target localization and online Milestone Coverage, illustrating how DashAct can guide practical agent improvements.
item.dc:creator: Chuhan Zhang, Qi Xie, Ziyue Wang, Jianing Yin, Yunfan Zhou, Dazhen Deng, Yingcai Wu

item.title: StructSim: Measuring Idea Similarity at Scale Through Structural Representation
item.description: arXiv:2609.34046v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Measuring idea similarity is fundamental to creativity evaluation, especially as LLMs enable idea generation at increasing scale. However, text embeddings collapse an idea into a single vector, making it difficult to capture structural similarity, including partial overlap across core and supporting components and differences across levels of abstraction. We introduce a shared structural representation that decomposes ideas into purpose, mechanism, and implementation components and organizes related components in a multi-layer concept graph. From this representation, we define measures of pairwise similarity and set-level mechanism coverage for assessing idea diversity. We evaluate our approach using controlled idea triples and assessments from 12 experts, focusing on differences in core mechanisms, implementations, and supporting components. Our method improves alignment with expert judgments of structural similarity by 31% over the embedding baseline and better reflects expert assessments of idea set coverage, supporting scalable evaluation of idea similarity and diversity.
item.dc:creator: Yaqing Yang, Vikram Mohanty, Mei-Xi Chia, Nikolas Martelaro, Dafna Shahaf, Aniket Kittur

item.title: Inflak: A Unified Orchestration Architecture for Human-Agent Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2610.21972v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-powered agents increasingly support open-ended activities, yet orchestrating when and how agents interact with humans remains challenging. Existing approaches often provide interaction mechanisms tied to particular tasks or execution patterns, lacking a unified architecture for diverse and evolving interaction needs. We introduce Inflak, a unified four-layer architecture for human-agent interaction orchestration that separates state reconstruction and routing, interaction and execution planning, interaction design, and interface rendering. Its layered design with progressive resolution enables general applicability, runtime flexibility, module composability, and orchestration maintainability. We implement Inflak as agent-native, skill-based plugins within a general-purpose agent framework and evaluate it through a gallery of various application scenarios and interaction paradigms, technical performance testing, and a comparative implementation case study. The evaluations show that Inflak can serve as a general and extensible foundation for orchestrating diverse human-agent interaction flows.
item.dc:creator: Lin Gao, Li Chen, Jianxun Lian, Ji Li, Haotian Li

item.title: ElectroCalm: Investigating User Experience and Physiological Responses to Multi-Node Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation for Stress Modulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.22748v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation (TES) for stress modulation has largely focused on vagus nerve stimulation at the neck, yet two questions remain underexplored: how users experience electrotactile sensations at this sensitive site, and whether electrotactile feedback itself can function as a haptic stress intervention. To investigate this gap, we applied an 8-node TES array to two body sites during a cognitively demanding 2-back task: the neck, a site used in prior vagal TES research for its anatomical proximity to the cervical vagus nerve, and the arm, the most common haptic wearable site, which primarily provides cutaneous electrotactile sensation without vagal access. In a usability study, both sites were rated as comparably comfortable without disrupting task performance, though the same stimulation was interpreted differently across sites. A second study assessing the physiological effects of active versus inactive stimulation under identical electrode attachment revealed that only neck TES produced cortical and autonomic changes consistent with stress modulation, while arm TES did not differ from inactive conditions. These findings suggest that neck TES can be acceptable despite the site's sensitivity, and that both the physiological effects and the sensory experience of TES depend on placement.
item.dc:creator: Yoon Kyung Shon, Pablo E. Paredes

item.title: AutoMind: Adaptive Knowledgeable Agent for Automated Data Science
item.description: arXiv:2506.10974v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown great potential in addressing real-world data science problems. LLM-driven data science agents promise to automate the entire machine learning pipeline, yet their real-world effectiveness remains limited. Existing frameworks depend on rigid, pre-defined workflows and inflexible coding strategies; consequently, they excel only on relatively simple, classical problems and fail to capture the empirical expertise that human practitioners bring to complex, innovative tasks. In this work, we introduce AutoMind, an adaptive, knowledgeable LLM-agent framework that overcomes these deficiencies through three key advances: (1) a curated expert knowledge base that grounds the agent in domain expert knowledge, (2) an agentic knowledgeable tree search algorithm that strategically explores possible solutions, and (3) a self-adaptive coding strategy that dynamically tailors code generation to task complexity. Evaluations on two automated data science benchmarks demonstrate that AutoMind delivers superior performance versus state-of-the-art baselines. Additional analyses confirm favorable effectiveness, efficiency, and qualitative solution quality, highlighting AutoMind as an efficient and robust step toward fully automated data science. Code is at https://github.com/zjunlp/AutoMind.
item.dc:creator: Yujie Luo, Yixin Ou, Jingsheng Zheng, Lanning Wei, Zhuoyun Yu, Shuofei Qiao, Jintian Zhang, Da Zheng, Yuren Mao, Yunjun Gao, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang

item.title: OUGS: Active View Selection via Object-aware Uncertainty Estimation in 3DGS
item.description: arXiv:2511.09397v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have achieved state-of-the-art results for novel view synthesis. However, efficiently capturing high-fidelity reconstructions of specific objects within complex scenes remains a significant challenge. A key limitation of existing active reconstruction methods is their reliance on scene-level uncertainty metrics, which are often biased by irrelevant background clutter and lead to inefficient view selection for object-centric tasks. We present OUGS, a novel framework that addresses this challenge with a more principled, physically-grounded uncertainty formulation for 3DGS. Our core innovation is to derive uncertainty directly from the explicit physical parameters of the 3D Gaussian primitives (e.g., position, scale, rotation). By propagating the covariance of these parameters through the rendering Jacobian, we establish a highly interpretable uncertainty model. This foundation allows us to then seamlessly integrate semantic segmentation masks to produce a targeted, object-aware uncertainty score that effectively disentangles the object from its environment. This allows for a more effective active view selection strategy that prioritizes views critical to improving object fidelity. Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the efficiency of the 3DGS reconstruction process and achieves higher quality for targeted objects compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, while also serving as a robust uncertainty estimator for the global scene.
item.dc:creator: Haiyi Li, Qi Chen, Denis Kalkofen, Hsiang-Ting Chen

item.title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
item.description: arXiv:2606.06271v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate writing feedback, there remains no systematic comparison of LLM and expert feedback on the dimensions that writing research identifies as central to revision: goal-orientation, anchoring to specific sentences, and prioritization. We introduce FOXGLOVE, a dataset of 696 feedback comments written by trained writing instructors on 69 twelfth-grade argumentative essays, paired with 1,644 comments generated from four frontier LLMs under a shared protocol, totaling 2,340 comments. We provide expert quality ratings on a subset of both instructor and LLM comments. We find that instructors and LLMs distribute feedback similarly across goals and essay positions, yet instructors and models diverge on the specific sentences on which to provide feedback. Additionally, we find that models tend to write more complex feedback and use fewer questions than instructors. LLM feedback also receives higher ratings on most dimensions of quality, as rated by instructors, but much of this advantage appears to be attributable to lengthier comments. FOXGLOVE enables systematic comparison of where human and LLM feedback align, diverge, and differ.
item.dc:creator: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August

item.title: EditPPT: Structured Execution and Evaluation for Reliable Slide Editing
item.description: arXiv:2608.20381v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable slide editing requires precise modifications to intended objects while preserving the rest of the presentation. We argue that slide editing is a problem of structured, constrained modification rather than open-ended code generation. Despite the complexity of real presentations, editing requests can largely be decomposed into the objects to change, the operations to apply, and the state to preserve. This perspective guides both evaluation and execution. For evaluation, we introduce DeckEdit-Bench, 183 editing tasks on 28 human-authored decks whose target and preserved objects are annotated at the shape level, so that intended and unintended changes are scored mostly by deterministic rules. For execution, we present EditPPT, a multi-agent framework that resolves targets before editing, restricts each specialist to a subset of 37 predefined tools, and validates each edit for instruction fulfillment and preservation, correcting or rolling back failed ones. Across five backbone models, EditPPT reaches 66.7-74.9% Task Success while keeping Preservation above 97%. Even with an open 27B model and no task-specific fine-tuning, it approaches Claude Code with Sonnet 5 in Task Success while better preserving the original deck. These results suggest that constraining how edits are executed, not only model scale, makes slide editing more reliable.
item.dc:creator: Jiheon Kim, Kyudan Jung, Jaegul Choo

item.title: Brain-to-Language Decoding: Paradigms, Signals, Methods, Evaluation, Practical Use and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2609.27650v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Brain-to-language decoding translates neural activity associated with language production, internal speech and perception into linguistic or expressive outputs. It offers a route to restoring communication after speech loss and a means of studying how the brain represents language. Advances in neural recording and representation learning have expanded the field from constrained recognition and acoustic reconstruction to text generation, streaming personalised speech and facial animation. This survey synthesises these developments across invasive and non-invasive measurements. We connect Articulated, Inner and Perceived paradigms to the neural populations they engage, the representations available to decoders and the outputs those representations can support. We examine model development, public resources and the evolution of evaluation, and compare published performance and communication costs within their reported protocols. The synthesis identifies complementary routes to progress: phonetic, acoustic and semantic targets preserve different aspects of a message; shared representations support reuse across recording conditions and tasks; and online communication increasingly depends on calibration, feedback and user control alongside decoding accuracy. Shared benchmarks enable algorithmic comparisons, while longitudinal studies reveal the demands of sustained use. We discuss these developments and their remaining limitations, then outline a prospective five-level trajectory from commands and language to meaning, scenarios and bidirectional cognitive exchange.
item.dc:creator: Yiqian Yang, Yiqun Duan, Chenyu Liu, Yiqi Wang, Xinliang Zhou, Chin-Teng Lin, Yu Zhang

item.title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2610.15136v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users rely on them appropriately. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models large-world decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.
item.dc:creator: Michaela Benk, Kacper Sokol

item.title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
item.description: arXiv:2610.15231v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.
item.dc:creator: Jiawei Xiong, Cheng Tang, Hong Jiao, Hanna Choi

item.title: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
item.description: arXiv:2610.23144v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.
item.dc:creator: Zhiqing Guo, Lixin Jia, Luning Sun, Xiaowei Chen, Guofeng Yu, Liejun Wang, Gaobo Yang, David Stillwell, Thorsten Holz, Shujun Li

item.title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
item.description: arXiv:2610.23284v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $\kappa = 0.82$.
item.dc:creator: Arun Josephraj Arokiaraj, Chenyi Huang, Bin Wu, Sahan Bulathwela
